Assumption: RGDU formula: minimum rate 0.02; size adjustment 0.3781 / 0.3821; zero from 3 minimum wages
Justification: Decree no. 2025-887

Assumption: Legacy relief: 0.3193 / 0.3233; health contribution relief to 2.396 minimum wages; family benefits to 3.354
Justification: Tissot (2025); Legisocial and Previssima

Assumption: Reference firm sizes: 27 / 553 / 13,321 employees, used for the 50-employee threshold
Justification: Insee, firms by size category, 2023

Assumption: Median and 90th-percentile net wages: 2,190 and 4,334 euros
Justification: Insee survey no. 2079

Assumption: Wages by sector are proportional to the sector's average wage
Justification: Insee dataset 2381338

Assumption: Near-minimum-wage profile set to 1.2 minimum wages
Justification: DGT guide (2024, pp. 14, 16); CGT document (2018) is a policy claim, not an observed value

Assumption: Wage level proxies qualification: below high school, high school, and post-secondary
Justification: DGT guide (2024): job classification relates education and minimum pay; simplified by the project

Assumption: Employee shares by wage level: 39 / 42 / 19 percent
Justification: Insee survey no. 2132 (2025), figure 3

Assumption: Economy scaled to one hundredth: one simulated employee represents 100 actual employees
Justification: Used to keep the model fast; results are multiplied by 100

Assumption: Employees are represented as firm-level counts, not individual agents
Justification: Simplification; unemployed people are represented as agents

Assumption: Unemployment rates by qualification: 14.7 / 9.1 / 5.3 percent
Justification: Insee Reference Series,  2026, unemployment inequalities (2025)

Assumption: Vacancy rate of 2.3 percent; vacancies are allocated by separation rates
Justification: Dares Focus no. 33 (2024)

Assumption: Sector separation rate based on annual permanent-contract endings divided by four
Justification: Dares 2025 contract endings; Insee employment

Assumption: About one third of separations lead to unemployment
Justification: Insee Reference Series,  2025: 1.8 percent of employees move to unemployment per quarter

Assumption: Unemployment-to-inactivity transition: 22.7 percent per quarter
Justification: Insee Reference Series,  2025, labor market transitions (2024)

Assumption: Inactivity-to-unemployment transition: 5.8 percent per quarter
Justification: Insee Reference Series,  2025, labor market transitions (2024)

Assumption: Initial inactive population balances transitions; total employees, unemployed and inactive people is conserved
Justification: The inactive population is unavailable for the six sectors; this affects the source of new hires

Assumption: Employer contributions set to 41 percent of gross wages
Justification: Inspired by Albertini et al. (2025); other references suggest 44 to 47 percent

Assumption: Employment elasticity: -0.4 at minimum wage, zero at 2 minimum wages, plus mu = -0.2
Justification: Bozio and Wasmer (2024), p. 194

Assumption: Cobb-Douglas matching function with unemployed-worker exponent 0.5
Justification: Petrongolo and Pissarides (2001)

Assumption: Unemployed agents' hiring weight falls by 45 percent after three quarters
Justification: Kroft, Lange and Notowidigdo (2013)

Assumption: Long-term unemployment means four quarters or more
Justification: Insee (one year); used for validation, not calibration

Assumption: Firms lay off 25 percent of excess employment each quarter
Justification: Hamermesh and Pfann (1996); Bentolila and Bertola (1990)

Assumption: Recruitment effort can fill vacancies faster but uses resources
Justification: Davis, Faberman and Haltiwanger (2013); Gavazza, Mongey and Violante (2018)

Assumption: Effort increases total labor-market matches according to the average weight of open vacancies
Justification: Inspired by Davis et al. (2013); exact functional form is a project assumption

Assumption: Effort advantage 0.5; effort penalty 0.10
Justification: Not directly supported by a source; tested in sensitivity analysis

Assumption: Firms learn through reinforcement and explore randomly in 10 percent of periods
Justification: Brenner (2006); Roth and Erev (1995)

Assumption: Learning gain 0.10; exploration rate 10 percent
Justification: Not directly supported by a source

Assumption: Baseline scenario disables learning; alternative scenario enables it
Justification: Instructor instruction to compare baseline and alternative scenarios

Assumption: Severe GDP scenario reproduces the observed 2026 shortfall of about 1.3 percent
Justification: Insee, Rapid Information bulletin no. 263 (30 October 2026)

Assumption: Central GDP scenario grows by 0.4 percent per quarter
Justification: Project scenario

Assumption: Sector demand sensitivity ranges from 0.9 to 1.2
Justification: Project scenario

Assumption: Expectations are smoothed using alpha = 0.4
Justification: Instructor model parameter EXPECTATION_ADJUSTMENT

Assumption: Thirty-six firm archetypes: six sectors by six profiles
Justification: Project design choice

Assumption: Results report simulation means and 95-percent confidence intervals using common random seeds
Justification: Course guidance: account for simulation randomness; use the same seeds across scenarios
